summary: This standards-track memo defines MIB objects for managing RADIUS authentication servers. It replaces RFC 2619 by deprecating the table limited to IPv4 addresses and adding a new one using version-neutral IP addresses, and adds UNITS and REFERENCE clauses to some objects.

eli5.summary: A RADIUS server decides who gets in. This gives network managers a dashboard to watch that decision-maker, now working with both old and new style addresses.

subtitle: The SNMP counters a RADIUS authentication server keeps about itself and each client, redone so they work with IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The earlier RADIUS authentication server MIB (RFC 2619) identified each client with an IPv4-only address object, so it could not describe clients reached over IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4669 deprecates the IPv4-only client table and adds radiusAuthClientExtTable, which stores the client address as a version-neutral type plus address pair. The remaining objects are carried forward, with UNITS and REFERENCE clauses added to some.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2619. The old table may still be supported for IPv4-only entities or older management stations, while IPv6-capable implementations use the new one.

today: RFC 4669 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2619, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. Its client-side companion is RFC 4668.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4669 defines a piece of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing a RADIUS authentication server, as RADIUS is defined in RFC 2865. Management stations read the objects through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and the module is written in the SMIv2 format.

In RADIUS authentication, clients send Access-Requests, and servers reply with Access-Accepts, Access-Rejects and Access-Challenges. Servers are expected to implement this MIB, while NAS devices that act as clients implement the client MIB in RFC 4668. An entity that does both, such as a RADIUS proxy, is expected to support both MIBs.
sections.eli5: A RADIUS server is the person who checks the guest list. This document is the set of gauges a manager can read to see how busy that person is and what answers they are giving.

sections.title: Why a New Table Was Needed
sections.content:
The old table from RFC 2619, radiusAuthClientTable, stored each client address in an IpAddress object, which only holds IPv4. RFC 4669 deprecates that table and adds radiusAuthClientExtTable, which uses radiusAuthClientInetAddressType and radiusAuthClientInetAddress to support version-neutral addresses.

The RFC follows the advice in RFC 4001: when revising a MIB that has IPv4-specific tables, define new tables with the version-neutral textual conventions, set their status to current, and change the old tables to deprecated. Maintaining several similar tables for different IP versions is strongly discouraged.
sections.eli5: The old guest list only had room for the short, old-style address. The new one has a spot saying which kind of address it is and a roomier spot to write it.

sections.title: Server Scalars and the Client Table
sections.content:
The module has fourteen scalars plus one table. The scalars describe the server as a whole: an identification string for the server software (the text gives FNS-2.1 as an example), how long the server process has been running, and the time since its last reset. They also include radiusAuthServConfigReset and totals for requests, invalid requests, duplicate requests, accepts, rejects, challenges, malformed requests, bad authenticators, dropped packets and unknown types.

The table has one row for each RADIUS authentication client with which the server shares a secret. Each row of the new table is indexed by radiusAuthClientExtIndex, a number from 1 to 2147483647. It holds the client's address type and address, its NAS-Identifier (radiusAuthClientExtID, not necessarily the same as sysName in MIB II), and per-client counters for the same kinds of packet that the totals cover. A final object, radiusAuthServCounterDiscontinuity, gives the centiseconds since the last discontinuity in the server counters, for example after the server module is reinitialized.

The counters are related by simple arithmetic written in the module's comments. For example, responses equal accepts plus rejects plus challenges, and requests minus duplicates, bad authenticators, malformed requests, unknown types, dropped packets and responses leaves the pending requests.
sections.eli5: The server keeps one big tally for everything it has seen, plus a separate row of tally marks for each client that talks to it.

sections.title: Reset and the Deprecated Table
sections.content:
One scalar, radiusAuthServConfigReset, is writable. The only value that can be set is reset(2), which reinitializes any persistent server state as if the server had just been started. When read, it returns other(1), initializing(3) or running(4).

A managed entity MAY keep supporting the deprecated table if it only supports IPv4, or if it supports both IPv4 and IPv6 and wants backwards compatibility with older management stations. The second option SHOULD only be used when the addresses in the new table are IPv4 and can be shown accurately in both tables.

Entities SHOULD NOT create rows in the old table for clients whose address is not IPv4, and SHOULD NOT return inaccurate addresses or SNMP access errors for the IPv4-only objects. When both tables describe the same client, the row indexes SHOULD match so management applications can correlate them.
sections.eli5: There is one big red button that restarts the server's counting, and it is the only thing a manager may change. The old guest list may stay for people who only read old-style addresses, as long as it never shows a wrong address.

sections.title: Compliance and Groups
sections.content:
The deprecated compliance statement is for IPv4-only entities or backwards-compatible use. The current one is for entities that support IPv6, or IPv4 and IPv6, and requires the extended object group. In it, radiusAuthServConfigReset is described as having reset(2) as the only SETable value.

For the new statement, an implementation is only required to support IPv4 and globally unique IPv6 addresses. The address type is limited to ipv4(1) and ipv6(2), and the address size to 4 or 16 octets.
sections.eli5: There is a checklist for the old gauges and a newer one for the new gauges. The newer one only asks for the two common kinds of address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unlike the client MIB, this module does have a writable object. radiusAuthServConfigReset can reinitialize the server's persistent state. Depending on the implementation, that may or may not interrupt pending requests, and abuse of it may lead to a Denial of Service attack on the server.

The client address objects could also help an attacker, because they reveal the authentication clients the server is talking to. The RFC says it is important to control even GET access and possibly to encrypt the values on the wire.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 do not provide a secure environment. The RFC RECOMMENDS considering the SNMPv3 security features and says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The restart button is dangerous in the wrong hands, and the list of clients could help a bad guy, so only trusted people should be allowed to press or peek.
